chapterTitle: Organ Donations: The Default Solution Illusion

facts.claim: Johnson and Goldstein reported donor-registration figures near 12 percent in Germany and 99.98 percent in Austria.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because germany required an affirmative opt-in while Austria treated nonresponse as donor status.
facts.commonError: The figures directly measure completed organ transplants.
facts.whyWrong: They describe recorded consent or non-objection, not clinical recovery.

facts.claim: Wales introduced soft deemed consent in 2015 and England's law took effect in May 2020.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because the legal default changed while family consultation remained part of practice.
facts.commonError: Opt-out law authorizes routine recovery without contacting relatives.
facts.whyWrong: The systems are explicitly soft and families are consulted.

facts.claim: US driver's-license and state-ID processes helped build donor registries covering roughly 170 million people.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because a common recurring transaction prompts an explicit answer and makes registration immediate.
facts.commonError: Prompted choice can reach only people who visit transplant hospitals.
facts.whyWrong: Motor-vehicle agencies contact a far broader population.

facts.claim: Presumed consent is a weaker signal of personal preference than an explicit recorded yes.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because silence can result from inattention, ignorance, or inertia rather than endorsement.
facts.commonError: Failure to opt out proves considered support for donation.
facts.whyWrong: Nonresponse does not reveal why the person stayed with the default.

facts.claim: Prompted choice asks for a decision without presuming that silence reveals consent.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because the prompt raises attention and records the answer the person actually supplies.
facts.commonError: Prompted choice requires coercing everyone to become a donor.
facts.whyWrong: A no remains available and can be recorded as clearly as a yes.

facts.claim: First-person authorization gives a registered donor decision legal force after death.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because procurement teams can rely on the individual's documented permission rather than treating it as an informal indication.
facts.commonError: A registry entry is always legally meaningless once family members object.
facts.whyWrong: State laws can make the donor's authorization binding, though teams still manage family conflict in practice.

facts.claim: Soft opt-out may not increase donation if families refuse or cannot be consulted.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because organ recovery depends on cooperation, medical suitability, timing, and clinical capacity beyond the legal default.
facts.commonError: Changing one form's default mechanically produces more transplantable organs.
facts.whyWrong: The clinical pathway contains several later gates.

facts.claim: Family knowledge of the deceased person's wishes strengthens the donation decision.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because a clear prior conversation reduces uncertainty during acute bereavement.
facts.commonError: Registry design makes family communication irrelevant.
facts.whyWrong: Families remain central in soft systems and in clinical practice.

facts.claim: Organ-donation design must consider recipients, potential donors, donor families, and clinicians.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because a policy that maximizes one group's outcome can impose consent uncertainty or operational burden on another.
facts.commonError: The number of people on the waiting list is the only relevant policy criterion.
facts.whyWrong: Autonomy, bereavement, and safe clinical execution also matter.

allowedAnchors.label: prompted organ-donor choice
allowedAnchors.text: People are directly asked to record yes or no at a natural administrative touchpoint, with registration made simple. An explicit signal helps families and clinicians honor a person's preference while overcoming procrastination.
